name: nemeton

attributes.attribute: Gaulish word for sacred grove or sanctuary
later site of a Benedictine priory in south-western Brittany

sources: Cunliffe, Barry. The Ancient Celts. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997), 198.
Lonigan, Paul R. The Druids: Priests of the Ancient Celts. Contributions to the Study of Religion, No. 45. Westport, Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1996, 3.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The nemeton was a sacred grove or sanctuary. The term comes from Gaulish and ties to outdoor rites of the Celts. Worship took place outside rather than inside buildings. Trees carried deep religious weight in such clearings. The word links to old European roots. Greek nemos names a glade. Latin nemus names what is sacred. An older Irish root nem covers heaven and holy things. Greek and Roman writers set the image. Strabo recorded oak groves where Galatian clans gathered. The poet Lucan gave a darker picture, with rough wooden figures seated in deep shade. Fire or earth-shaking might touch a nemeton. Yet the trees stayed whole. After Roman rule spread, the same word named stone shrines. It also named whole towns. Medionemeton in what is now Scotland took the name that way. A medieval forest called Nemeton sat near Locronan. Locronan lies in south-western Brittany. A Benedictine priory later rose within those bounds.

okr.objective: Define the nemeton as a Gaulish word for a sacred grove and trace how it named Celtic ritual sites, Roman-era stone shrines, and later Christian foundations.
key_results: The nemeton was a Gaulish term for a sacred grove or sanctuary.
Greek nemos, Latin nemus, and Old Irish nem mark the wider Indo-European roots.
Strabo and Lucan described the oak groves used by Galatian and other Celtic worshippers.
Medionemeton in Scotland shows the term naming a Roman-era settlement.
A medieval sacred forest called Nemeton lay near Locronan in south-western Brittany and hosted a Benedictine priory.
